L6.1.quote: Choose the unique $n$ for which $a_n<x\le a_{n+1}$. Since $x\in S$, it has gcd greater than $1$ with each of $a_1,\ldots,a_n$. The minimality in the definition of $a_{n+1}$ therefore gives $a_{n+1}\le x$. Hence $x=a_{n+1}$.
L6.1.note: Both directions present: pairwise gcd>1 of terms noted; minimality shows any x>=a_1 non-coprime to all terms is a term. Valid.

L6.2.quote: Let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty, possibly infinite family of nonempty finite subsets of a set $P$. If every two members of $\mathcal F$ intersect, then there are finitely many nonempty finite sets $B_1,\ldots,B_s\subseteq P$
L6.2.note: Lemma is false: F_k={x_1..x_k,y_k} is pairwise intersecting with infinitely many minimal transversals; induction only handles transversals meeting C, which fails recursively.

L6.3.quote: Take $y=a_n$. Then $a_n+L\in S$, and among the integers strictly greater than $a_n$ and at most $a_n+L$ there are exactly $T$ members of $S$.
L6.3.note: Assembly for all n>=1 is conditionally correct, but S, b_j, L all rest on the false transversal lemma, so nothing is established.

parsed.notes: Core finiteness comes from a false lemma: pairwise-intersecting families of finite sets need not have finitely based transversals ({x_1..x_k,y_k} counterexample); the proof's induction silently assumes every transversal meets C, which fails in recursive calls. Only the characterization (C) survives; wrong_answer_stated: proof relies on a false lemma.
